x: The particle (photon) nature of light explains the photoelectric and Compton effects. Interference, diffraction and polarisation need the wave nature instead.
t: Discriminate effects explained by wave nature from those explained by particle nature.

x: Option B is incorrect: the normal is perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence, not parallel. The other statements are the laws of reflection.
t: Recall the laws of reflection and the meaning of "normal".

x: A rough surface scatters rays in many directions, giving irregular or diffused reflection with no clear image. Smooth mirrors give regular (specular) reflection.
t: Discriminate regular from diffused reflection.

x: Both are true and R explains A: when light goes from denser to rarer medium beyond the critical angle, all of it is reflected back, which is total internal reflection.
t: Recall the two conditions for TIR.

x: A plane mirror is used in periscopes, a concave mirror for shaving, a convex mirror for security, and a convex mirror as a vehicle rear-view mirror, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall one use of each mirror type.

x: A plane mirror gives an image the same size and erect, so m = +1. Negative magnification would mean an inverted real image.
t: Recall the sign convention for magnification.

x: Option D is incorrect: an object inside F of a concave mirror gives a virtual, erect, magnified image, not an inverted one. The other statements are true.
t: Check each mirror case for real/inverted versus virtual/erect.

x: Statement A is true: frequency stays the same while speed and wavelength change. Statement B is false: refraction comes from a change in speed between media of different optical density, not intensity.
t: Recall what changes and what stays fixed in refraction.

x: Lenses converge or diverge light, prisms deviate and disperse it, optical fibres transmit signals and spectacles correct eye defects, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the function of each optical device.

x: Both are true and R explains A: total internal reflection keeps light in the core, so signals travel far with low loss and high bandwidth.
t: Check whether R is the principle behind A.

x: I and II are correct: optical fibres and diamond sparkle use total internal reflection. III is false because a mirage comes from TIR in hot air layers, not from a mirror.
t: Recall the examples of total internal reflection.

x: An endoscope views organs through fibres, a mirage is TIR in air layers, a diamond shows multiple TIR, and a Porro prism inverts images without loss, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall each TIR application.

x: Option D is incorrect: a concave lens is diverging; a convex lens is converging. Cylindrical lenses correct astigmatism.
t: Discriminate convex (converging) from concave (diverging) lenses.

x: Lens power is measured in dioptres; P = 1/f with f in metres.
t: Recall P = 1/f (metres) in dioptres.

x: Both are true and R explains A: within F a convex lens gives a virtual, erect, magnified image, which is how a magnifying glass works.
t: Check whether R is the use that follows from A.

x: The cornea does most of the refraction, the iris controls pupil size, the retina is the screen and the optic nerve carries signals to the brain, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the function of each eye part.

x: I, II and III are correct: myopia blurs distant objects, hypermetropia blurs near ones and presbyopia is age-related loss of accommodation. IV is false: lens clouding is cataract, while astigmatism is uneven curvature.
t: Discriminate astigmatism from cataract.

x: Option D is incorrect: myopia is corrected with a concave lens of negative power, not positive. The image forms in front of the retina.
t: Recall the lens and power sign for each defect.

x: Both are true: a convex lens corrects hypermetropia and a cylindrical lens corrects astigmatism.
t: Recall the corrective lens for each eye defect.

x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct: the normal near point is 25 cm, closer in myopia and farther in hypermetropia. Statement 4 is false because the normal far point is infinity.
t: Discriminate near point (25 cm) from far point (infinity).

x: Sunlight enters a drop, refracts and disperses, reflects totally inside the back of the drop, and refracts out, giving A, B, C, D.
t: Recall rainbow formation: refraction, dispersion, TIR, refraction.

x: Violet has the shortest wavelength and the highest refractive index in glass, so it deviates most. Red deviates least.
t: Recall that deviation rises as wavelength falls.

x: Both are true and R explains A: air molecules scatter short blue wavelengths far more than red (Rayleigh scattering), so the sky looks blue.
t: Recall that Rayleigh scattering varies as 1/λ⁴.

x: I, II and III are correct: stars twinkle and the Sun appears early and sets late because of atmospheric refraction, and planets don't twinkle because they look like discs. IV is false because a mirage is TIR, not scattering.
t: Discriminate refraction effects from scattering and TIR effects.

x: Both are true and R explains A: light shows wave behaviour and also behaves as photons, which is what dual nature means.
t: Check whether R defines A.

x: All three are explained by the wave nature of light: interference, diffraction and polarisation.
t: Discriminate wave-nature effects from particle-nature effects.

x: Both are true: an EM wave has electric and magnetic fields vibrating at right angles to its motion, and it needs no medium.
t: Recall EM waves as transverse and medium-free.

x: Light is fastest in a vacuum at about 3 × 10⁸ m/s and slows in air, water and glass as optical density rises.
t: Recall that light is slower in denser media.

x: Glass, water and air are transparent, frosted glass and butter paper translucent, and wood, metal and stone opaque, while light travels freely in a vacuum, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Discriminate transparent, translucent and opaque materials.

x: All five are correct: smooth surfaces such as mirrors give regular reflection and a clear image, while walls and paper give irregular reflection.
t: Discriminate regular from diffused reflection.

x: All four are correct: a plane mirror's image is virtual, erect, the same size and laterally inverted.
t: Recall the image properties of a plane mirror.

x: Plane mirrors serve as looking glasses and in kaleidoscopes, and concave mirrors in headlights and telescopes, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the uses of plane and concave mirrors.

x: A concave mirror focuses sunlight at its focus in solar cookers and furnaces. Security, street-lamp and rear-view mirrors are convex.
t: Discriminate concave (converging) from convex (diverging) mirror uses.

x: All five are correct uses of concave mirrors: shaving and makeup mirrors, headlights, solar cookers, torches and searchlights, and dentists' mirrors.
t: Recall the uses of concave mirrors.

x: Convex mirrors serve street lamps, give a wide rear view in vehicles, cover large areas in shops and widen the view at ATMs and parking areas, giving a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall the uses of convex mirrors.

x: Both are true: a convex rear-view mirror gives an erect, diminished image, and a convex street-light reflector spreads light over a wide area.
t: Recall convex mirror images and uses.

x: Both are true and R is taken to explain A, since R restates that a large aperture and no chromatic aberration are the defining traits of a reflecting telescope.
t: Check whether R restates the reason for A.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: equal object and image distance comes from the laws of reflection, not from lateral inversion.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true: cameras and microscopes form images with lenses, and refraction makes objects in water look raised (apparent depth).
t: Recall the applications of refraction.

x: All four are correct: TIR needs light going from denser to rarer medium beyond the critical angle, no refraction occurs, and ideally all the light is reflected.
t: Recall the conditions and features of TIR.

x: The core has the higher refractive index and the cladding the lower, the fibre has a core-and-cladding structure, and i > C is needed at the interface, giving a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
t: Recall why the core is denser than the cladding.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: fibres resist interference because they carry light, not electric current, while their use in telecom is a consequence.
t: Check whether R is the cause or merely a use.

x: Internet, telephone services and cable TV are all applications of optical-fibre telecommunication, which is signal transmission, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall that the code pairs items in order when List-II repeats.

x: Endoscopy lets doctors view internal organs, fibres deliver lasers precisely in surgery, and fibre sensors measure temperature and pressure, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the medical and sensing uses of optical fibres.

x: Both are true: fibre sensors measure strain, and fibres give lightweight data links in military aircraft.
t: Recall the uses of optical fibres.

x: Optical fibres carry light for decorative and medical illumination. Pupil control, eye correction and dispersion belong to the eye, lenses and prisms.
t: Recall the uses of optical fibres.

x: An endoscope works by TIR in fibre bundles: one bundle gives illumination, another carries the image back, and flexibility lets it enter body cavities, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall how the two fibre bundles in an endoscope work.

x: Both are true: a flexible endoscope enters body cavities, allowing internal viewing with little or no surgery.
t: Recall the advantages of endoscopy.

x: An inferior mirage is the desert type, a superior mirage comes from cold air layers, hot air near the ground has lower refractive index, and all mirages need refractive index to change steadily with height, giving a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
t: Discriminate inferior (hot ground) from superior (cold air) mirages.

x: Both statements are true: a mirage shows an inverted image of a distant object and looks like water, so the answer is "only two".
t: Check each statement about mirages.

x: Diamond's refractive index is about 2.42 and its critical angle about 24.4°; its brilliance comes from TIR and dispersion, and facets are cut to maximise TIR, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall diamond's refractive index and critical angle.

x: Diamond's critical angle is very small (about 24°), so most light inside meets the faces beyond it and is totally internally reflected, making it sparkle.
t: Recall that a high refractive index gives a small critical angle.

x: All four are correct: concavo-convex (thicker centre) is a convex lens, while double-concave, plano-concave and convexo-concave are concave lenses.
t: Recall that a lens thicker at the centre is convex.

x: Both are true: bifocal lenses have two zones for near and far vision, and progressive lenses blend the two powers smoothly.
t: Recall multi-power spectacle lenses.

x: All four are correct: beyond 2F the image is diminished, at 2F same size, between F and 2F magnified (all real and inverted), and at F it is at infinity, highly magnified.
t: Recall convex lens images as the object moves closer.

x: Both are true and R explains A: a concave lens always spreads rays apart, so for any object position the image is virtual, erect and diminished.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: All seven are correct: convex lenses in projectors and the eye, concave lenses in peepholes and door viewers, and lens combinations in microscopes, telescopes and binoculars.
t: Recall the uses of each lens type.

x: Both are true: a camera forms a real inverted image on film or sensor, and the objective of a microscope or telescope forms a real image.
t: Recall where convex lenses form real images.

x: A projector places the slide between F and 2F of a convex lens, so it throws a magnified real image on the screen.
t: Recall convex lens image cases.

x: The eye lens focuses a real, inverted image on the retina, which acts as the screen. The cornea refracts and the iris controls the pupil.
t: Recall the role of each part of the eye.

x: A burning glass is a convex lens that converges sun rays to a point and can ignite paper.
t: Recall that a convex lens converges light.

x: A concave lens corrects myopia by diverging rays, a peephole gives a wide view, Galilean telescopes use a concave eyepiece, and concave lenses correct some aberrations, giving a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
t: Recall the uses of concave lenses.

x: The cornea gives about 70% of focusing, the iris controls the light let in, the pupil is the opening, and the lens fine-tunes focus, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
t: Recall the function of each front eye structure.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the ciliary muscles change the curvature of the eye lens, and that change is what accommodation is.
t: Check whether R is the mechanism of A.

x: All three are correct: the retina has rods and cones, and both the aqueous and vitreous humours keep the eye's shape and help refract light.
t: Recall the structures inside the eye.

x: All five are correct: hypermetropia is long-sightedness, colour blindness is a cone defect, myopia comes from a long eyeball or too much converging power, and it is corrected by a diverging lens such as −2 D.
t: Recall the cause and correction of each eye defect.

x: Both are true: in hypermetropia a short eyeball or weak converging power makes the image form behind the retina.
t: Discriminate myopia (image in front) from hypermetropia (image behind).

x: Both are true and R explains A: a convex lens converges the rays to pull the image forward onto the retina, so its power is positive.
t: Check whether R is why the power is positive.

x: Hypermetropia is corrected with a convex lens, so its power is positive, such as +2 D. −2 D would correct myopia.
t: Recall the power sign for each eye defect.

x: Presbyopia comes from weak ciliary muscles and a stiff lens, so the near point recedes. It is corrected by bifocal or progressive lenses with a convex near portion, and old age often combines myopia with hypermetropia. This gives a-v, b-iii, c-ii, d-i, e-iv.
t: Recall the cause, effect and correction of presbyopia.

x: Option C is incorrect: astigmatism is corrected with cylindrical or toric lenses or surgery, not spherical contact lenses only. The other statements on irregular curvature and blurring are true.
t: Check each statement for the word "only".

x: Two are correct: the near point is the closest distance of clear vision, also called the least distance of distinct vision. 3 describes the far point, and the normal near point is 25 cm, not 25 m.
t: Discriminate near point from far point and check the units.

x: Both are true: the far point is the farthest clear-vision distance, and in myopia it is finite, nearer than infinity.
t: Recall how myopia shifts the far point.

x: In hypermetropia distant objects stay clear, so the far point remains infinity, but the near point moves beyond 25 cm and near vision blurs.
t: Discriminate which point each defect shifts.

x: Both are true and R explains A: accommodation is focusing at different distances, done by the ciliary muscles changing the lens curvature.
t: Check whether R is the mechanism of A.

x: All four are correct: for near objects the lens thickens and converges more, for far objects it thins, and the normal range runs from 25 cm to infinity.
t: Recall how the lens shape changes with distance.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the Sun behind the observer is only the viewing condition, while refraction, dispersion and TIR in drops make the rainbow.
t: Check whether R is a cause or only a condition.

x: A primary rainbow uses one TIR in each drop, a secondary uses two, and the secondary has reversed colours and is fainter, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Discriminate primary from secondary rainbows.

x: All three are correct: each wavelength refracts differently, so a primary rainbow has red on the outside and violet on the inside.
t: Recall the colour order in a primary rainbow.

x: Red has the lowest refractive index and deviates least, a spectrum is continuous, and the continuous spectrum is VIBGYOR, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall red as least deviated and violet as most.

x: A prism spectrometer gives a pure spectrum, a rainbow is a natural spectrum, chromatic aberration is a lens defect and an achromatic doublet reduces it, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the applications and defects of dispersion.

x: Both are true: spectroscopy analyses light from stars and elements, and diamond's fire is dispersion of white light.
t: Recall the applications of dispersion.

x: Both are correct: Rayleigh scattering is by particles much smaller than the wavelength, and its intensity varies as 1/λ⁴.
t: Discriminate Rayleigh (small particles) from Mie (large particles).

x: A medium with a higher refractive index is optically denser, so light travels more slowly in it. Optical density differs from opacity.
t: Discriminate optical density from mass density and opacity.

x: Prisms in binoculars and periscopes reflect by TIR without silvering, road-sign reflectors give high visibility, and dew drops sparkle by TIR, giving a-iii, b-i, c-ii.
t: Recall the applications of TIR.

x: A camera, a compound microscope and a telescope all use convex lenses to form real images, so each pairs with (i).
t: Recall the lens type in each instrument.

x: Lens power is the reciprocal of focal length in metres, P = 1/f, measured in dioptres.
t: Recall P = 1/f.

x: All four are correct: Mie scattering is by larger particles such as cloud droplets and milk fat, and it scatters all colours equally, making clouds white.
t: Discriminate Mie (white) from Rayleigh (blue) scattering.

x: All four are correct: Rayleigh scattering reddens sunsets, high-frequency blue and violet scatter most, and the sky looks blue rather than violet because the eye is more sensitive to blue.
t: Recall why the sky is blue and not violet.

x: All four are correct: scattered light comes from every direction, at sunset light's long path scatters away blue, leaving red and orange, and dust deepens the red.
t: Recall why sunsets look red.

x: Both are true and R explains A: changes in air density give changes in refractive index, which bend light gradually.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: All three are correct: atmospheric refraction bends starlight at random, shifting stars' apparent positions and making their brightness flicker, which is twinkling.
t: Recall atmospheric refraction as the cause of twinkling.

x: Refraction bends sunlight over the horizon, so the Sun appears about two minutes before actual sunrise and stays about two minutes after sunset.
t: Recall advance sunrise and delayed sunset.

x: Both are true: atmospheric refraction shifts stars' apparent positions, and Rayleigh scattering gives the blue sky and red sunset.
t: Discriminate refraction effects from scattering effects.

x: Both are true and R explains A: light travels in straight lines, so the Moon or Earth casts a shadow, which is an eclipse.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: The critical angle is the incidence angle in the denser medium that gives 90° refraction, it is written C, depends on the pair of media and varies slightly with wavelength, giving a-iv, b-i, c-ii, d-iii.
t: Recall the definition and features of the critical angle.

x: Lens power is measured in dioptres, written D. C is the critical angle, λ is wavelength and n is refractive index.
t: Recall the symbol for each optics quantity.
